title: Generative Diffusion Prior Distillation for Long-Context Knowledge Transfer
one_liner: When a model must predict from partial sequences, a diffusion model learns to fill in missing information and shows the student many possible ways to complete the pattern.
lead: A typical time-series classifier sees the full sequence during training, but at test time must make a prediction from just the first few values. The classifier struggles because it was trained on patterns that live in the full sequence, not the partial one. This paper teaches a partial-sequence model by having a diffusion model imagine what the missing values could be, then showing the student several plausible versions of the full sequence to learn from.

paras: A time-series classifier is trained on complete sequences: stock prices from January to December, heart rates over a full hour, sensor readings from start to finish. It learns patterns that show up across the whole timeline. But at test time, latency and cost constraints mean you can only feed the first few values. The classifier now sees only January prices, only the first 10 minutes of heart rate, only the first few readings. The discriminative patterns (the features that actually tell the difference between classes) live in the full sequence, not the partial one, so accuracy drops sharply.

A beginner would try standard knowledge distillation: have a full-sequence teacher model guide a partial-sequence student model by copying the teacher's learned features. But this backfires. The teacher's features are complex responses built from the entire sequence. The student's features come from a partial view. Forcing the student to match the teacher's full-context features is an impossible task—the student does not have the input information needed to produce those outputs.

callout.html: A model trained on complete sequences cannot simply copy a teacher trained on the same completeness into a student trained on partial sequences.

steps.b: Train a diffusion model on teacher features.
steps.text: Take the learned features from the teacher (full-sequence model) and train a diffusion model to restore a noisy, degraded version back to the original.
Think of the student's partial-sequence features as if they were the result of dropping out (removing) the information that the missing values would have contributed.
Use the diffusion model to imagine plausible full-sequence features that could have produced the observed partial features by reversing the degradation process iteratively.
Instead of one overwhelming target, the student now has several realistic versions of what the full-sequence features should look like.
Train the student to match all sampled versions, learning a mapping from partial to the set of plausible full-sequence behaviors.

paras: The paper changes the supervision signal seen by the student model. Instead of a single fixed target (the teacher's features), the student receives multiple diverse versions of plausible full-context features—all consistent with the partial information the student observes. This shift moves the learning problem from an impossible constraint (copy one overwhelming target) to a realistic one (learn the mapping between partial and multiple valid full versions).

hidden.h2: The Hidden Quantity: Plausible Full-Sequence Features
hidden.name: set of plausible full-context completions
paras: The key quantity the paper introduces is the set of plausible full-context features that could legitimately explain what the student observes. When the diffusion model samples (draws random instances from what it learned), it generates multiple realistic versions of how the full sequence should behave. Each sample is different, but all are consistent with the partial prefix the student sees and all carry the task-relevant patterns from the teacher. The student learns that partial data does not map to one answer but to multiple valid ones.

The diffusion model learns this by studying how teacher features degrade when you erase the contribution of missing time steps. Then it reverses that degradation process: given only what the partial sequence contributes, it restores plausible versions of what the missing context would have added. Each sample is a different but plausible completion drawn from what the diffusion model learned.

heat.caption: Darker means more important for distinguishing classes across many possible full-sequence versions.

reads.html: The diffusion model learns what a complete sequence looks like when you start with a partial one. Then it imagines several different ways the full sequence could complete. Each imagined completion is a different but reasonable guess.

GDPD learns a generative model (the diffusion model) over teacher features, then samples from it conditioned on the student's partial observations to generate a set of task-relevant target features for each example.

mechanism.h2: Why It Works: Diffusion Learns What Is Missing
paras: Standard knowledge distillation fails here because the student and teacher operate in different data regimes: the teacher saw complete sequences, the student sees partial ones. Forcing the student to exactly match the teacher's features is impossible—the student does not have the input information needed to produce those outputs. GDPD sidesteps this by asking a different question: not 'what is the one right target?' but 'what are all the plausible targets consistent with the partial information the student has?' A diffusion model is trained to answer this by learning to restore degraded (noisy) teacher features back to clean ones. This is exactly the skill needed: given only the partial-sequence contribution to the teacher's features, restore what the missing-sequence contribution would have added. When the diffusion model runs in reverse (denoising), it iteratively builds up a plausible completion. By sampling multiple times, you get multiple different completions, all reasonable. The student then learns to produce features that fit any of these possibilities. This teaches the student that partial data maps not to a single point but to a whole region: any of several valid behaviors could follow the same partial sequence.

The mechanism works because diffusion models excel at learning the shape of high-dimensional data. They see many examples of (full teacher features, ways to degrade them), and learn to invert that degradation. When you sample multiple times from the trained model, the outputs vary (different every time) but all stay true to what the model learned (all consistent with the observed partial data). This variation is critical: instead of one impossible target, the student sees many plausible ones, and learning to fit all of them teaches the student a useful skill.

stages.s: Student trained to match all sampled versions

math.h2: The Equation: Matching Multiple Plausible Targets
math.words: Student loss equals the negative log likelihood that the student's features came from the posterior distribution of plausible full features conditioned on observed partial features.
symbols: the loss (error) the student is minimizing
one sample of plausible full-context features from the posterior
the posterior distribution: what full features could explain the partial ones
the student model's output on partial input
squared distance (how far apart two feature vectors are)
average over many samples from the posterior distribution

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Student observes partial sequence with 4 values: x_partial = [5, 3, 8, 2].
Diffusion model posterior-samples 3 plausible full-sequence teacher features:
Student produces f_student(x_partial) = [1.1, 0.75, 1.57, 0.87, 1.13, 0.7, 2.27, 1.67, 0.5, 0.9, 1.8, 0.4] (average of the three targets).
The student learns a feature that sits in the center of the plausible region, making it easy to see the class-discriminative patterns.

math.note: The student minimizes squared error to the average of many posterior samples, learning to produce features consistent with all plausible full-sequence behaviors.

bars.h2: Comparing Approaches on a Time-Series Task

charts.title: Standard Knowledge Distillation
charts.note: Teacher features overwhelm the student; accuracy collapses on partial data.

charts.title: GDPD (This Paper)
charts.note: By learning to match multiple plausible targets, the student maintains strong accuracy even on partial data.

items.b: Diffusion model memorizes instead of generalizes.
items.html: If the diffusion model simply memorizes the training set, sampling produces copies of real examples rather than plausible new completions. The student then overfits to seen data. This happens if the diffusion model is not learned well enough or if you sample too few times.

If the diffusion model converges to a deterministic solution (very low variance), every sample is nearly identical. The student receives no diversity, and you lose the benefit of seeing multiple plausible targets. This often means the diffusion model is underfitting (not learning enough of the natural variation).

GDPD assumes a specific way that full-context features degrade to partial-context features. If the actual degradation is different (e.g., nonlinear or class-dependent), the diffusion model inverts the wrong process and produces irrelevant completions.

When the diffusion model is well-trained, each sampled completion differs in detail but all stay consistent with the partial input. The student receives multiple valid targets, and accuracy on partial data matches or approaches the full-sequence baseline.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Write a small time-series classifier on a standard benchmark (ECG, stocks, sensor data, anything with a natural train-full / test-partial split). Train a teacher on full sequences. Train a student on partial prefixes using standard KD, then using GDPD with posterior-sampling. Plot the accuracy on partial data as you vary the prefix length (how much of the sequence the student sees). GDPD should stay higher than standard KD across all prefix lengths, especially for very short prefixes. Also show that if you turn off posterior-sampling (use only one sample per student example), accuracy drops back toward standard KD, proving that diversity is what matters.
demo.metric_eq: accuracy_partial = (number of correct predictions on partial-sequence test set) / (total test examples)
demo.closing: The core proof is that the same student model achieves high accuracy on partial data when trained with diverse diffusion-sampled targets versus a single overwhelming teacher target.
